full_judgment:
6. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. Government and BCIC, contested the application by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations therein asserting that the application under section 233 of the Companies Act, 1994 was misconceived and untenable. It is also contended in the affidavit-in-opposition that when the government decided to sell 49% of the shares of the company to the public, the value of the assets of the company namely, the land, building, machinery and other moveable and immoveable assets including the good will of the company had substantially increased and consequently the market value of the shares also increased. Moreover, the company having been vested in respondent No. 2 for management started making profit. The government i.e. respondent No.1, in the circumstances, without taking away the profit which accrued to them after revaluation of the said assets of the company, in view of the financial position of the company, allowed the amount of profit to be retained by the company in the form of quasi-equity loan. The government did not charge any interest on the said quasi-equity loan from the company during the period from 1987-88 to 1991-92. The Government was justified in law to show the said profit accrued out of the revaluation of the fixed assets of the company as quasi equity loan amounting to Taka 12,26,36,225 and. as such, the issue of debentures in respect thereof and the creation of trust deed in this regard were in accordance with law. It is also contended by the respondent No. 1 that since the petitioner Nos. 1 to 4 in collusion with respondent No. 4 filed Title Suit No. 207 of 1993 for the same relief, which was still pending, the present application was not maintainable. It is further contended that the present application is also barred by limitation and hit by the principles of estoppel, acquiescence and waiver, inasmuch as the petitioners purchased the shares in 1989 on the basis of the prospectus of 1989 with knowledge of the said loan and they failed to challenge the same during the Annual General Meetings of the company or in any Court of law before the total disinvestment was made by the government in 1993. Respondent No. 2 BCIC also contested the application on the same ground by filing a separate affidavit-in-opposition. 

 23. Balance sheet, no doubt, is a good evidence of acknowledgment of any liability of the company. But the balance sheet should not be accepted as an acknowledgment if it is found that the directors or those who are in control of the company took decision favouring or in furtherance of their interest although that was to the detriment of the company and the minority shareholders. In Transplanters (holding Company) Ltd. (1958) 1 WLR 822 and Daniels and Others vs Daniels and Others (1978) 1 Ch. 406 may be referred to in this connection. Moreover, since the creation of the said quasi equity loan is not sustainable in law, question of limitation, estoppel or acquiescence cannot and in deed will not arise and the balance sheet will not provide an acknowledgment of any liability by the petitioners.
